git_lesson_1.title: Git Basics: Snapshots and Commits
git_lesson_1.description: Understand what Git tracks and create your first commit

git_lesson_1:slide:0.title: What is Git? 🌱
git_lesson_1:slide:0.content:
Git is a version control system. Think of it as a time machine for your project:

• Save checkpoints (commits)
• Go back safely
• Compare changes
• Collaborate without overwriting each other

git_lesson_1:slide:1.title: The 3 Core States
git_lesson_1:slide:1.content:
In beginner Git, you can imagine 3 layers:

1) Working files (what you edit)
2) Staging area (what you prepare)
3) Commit history (what you save forever)

git_lesson_1:slide:2.title: First Commit Flow
git_lesson_1:slide:2.content: A commit is a snapshot. Small, clear commits make projects easier to understand.

git_lesson_1:question:0.prompt: What is the main purpose of Git?
git_lesson_1:question:0.explanation: Git is for tracking file changes over time and coordinating work safely.

git_lesson_1:question:1.explanation: A commit is a saved snapshot of your code at a specific moment.

git_lesson_1:question:2.explanation: Use git commit with a message to create a new snapshot in history.

git_lesson_1:question:3.prompt: Why should commit messages be clear?
git_lesson_1:question:3.explanation: Good commit messages make project history readable for you and your team.

options.git_lesson_1:question:3:option:1: They help teammates understand what changed

git_lesson_2.title: Branches: Isolated Work
git_lesson_2.description: Create and switch branches to work safely in parallel

git_lesson_2:slide:0.title: Why Branches Matter 🌿
git_lesson_2:slide:0.content:
Branches let you test ideas without breaking your main line:

• main stays stable
• feature branches hold experiments
• merging later combines finished work

git_lesson_2:slide:1.title: Create and Move
git_lesson_2:slide:1.content: Use branch + checkout (or checkout -b) to create isolated workspaces.

git_lesson_2:slide:2.title: Shortcut: checkout -b
git_lesson_2:slide:2.content: Create and switch in one command. Great for fast feature starts.

git_lesson_2:question:0.prompt: What is the best reason to use a feature branch?
git_lesson_2:question:0.explanation: Branches isolate unfinished work and protect the stable branch.

git_lesson_2:question:1.prompt: What does git checkout -b feature do?
git_lesson_2:question:1.explanation: checkout -b is a shortcut for branch creation + switch.

options.git_lesson_2:question:1:option:1: Creates and switches to feature branch

git_lesson_2:question:2.prompt: After checkout to feature, where do new commits go?
git_lesson_2:question:2.explanation: Commits are attached to the currently checked-out branch.

git_lesson_2:question:3.prompt: Why keep main clean while learning?
git_lesson_2:question:3.explanation: A clean main branch makes project history and releases safer.

options.git_lesson_2:question:3:option:1: To keep stable progress and avoid confusion

git_lesson_3.title: Merge Fundamentals
git_lesson_3.description: Bring finished feature work back into main using merge commits

git_lesson_3:slide:0.title: What is Merge? 🔀
git_lesson_3:slide:0.content:
Merging combines histories from two branches.

When both branches moved, Git creates a merge commit with two parents.

git_lesson_3:slide:1.title: Basic Merge Workflow
git_lesson_3:slide:1.content: You usually merge into main after feature work is ready.

git_lesson_3:slide:2.title: Think in Graphs
git_lesson_3:slide:2.content: Git is a commit graph, not a folder copy. Branch names are movable labels pointing at commits.

git_lesson_3:question:0.prompt: What does git merge feature do from main?
git_lesson_3:question:0.explanation: Merge integrates another branch history into the current branch.

options.git_lesson_3:question:0:option:1: Moves feature to main without history

git_lesson_3:question:1.prompt: Where should you be before merging feature into main?
git_lesson_3:question:1.explanation: You merge into the branch you currently have checked out.

git_lesson_3:question:2.explanation: A merge commit connects two lines of history.

options.git_lesson_3:question:2:option:1: A commit with exactly one parent
options.git_lesson_3:question:2:option:2: A commit with two parents joining histories

git_lesson_3:question:3.explanation: Seeing the graph makes branch movement and merges easier to reason about.

git_lesson_4.title: Beginner Branch Workflow Mission
git_lesson_4.description: Practice an end-to-end branch workflow using checkout -b and merge

git_lesson_4:slide:0.title: Daily Workflow Pattern
git_lesson_4:slide:0.content:
A practical beginner flow:

1) Start from main
2) Create branch with checkout -b
3) Commit feature work
4) Return to main
5) Merge branch

git_lesson_4:slide:1.title: Why this works
git_lesson_4:slide:1.content: This workflow keeps changes focused, reviewable, and easy to rollback if needed.

git_lesson_4:slide:2.title: Mission Commands
git_lesson_4:slide:2.content: Use this exact idea in your final beginner challenge.

git_lesson_4:question:1.explanation: You merge after implementing and committing feature work.
